scenario: Your project team has a major deadline in two days. Two key team members are strongly disagreeing on how to format the final presentation, causing work to stall completely.
question: How would you handle this situation?
options: Intervene immediately, listen to both viewpoints objectively, and propose a compromise combining the strengths of both formats.
Call a quick team vote and move forward with the format preferred by the majority to avoid wasting time.
Take charge, select the format you believe is most practical, and assign clear completion tasks to both members.
Let the two members debate and work it out themselves so that ownership and team trust remain intact.

scenario: During an academic competition or group assignment, you discover that a member of your group unintentionally included uncredited, plagiarised content from an online source.
question: What is your immediate response?
options: Privately inform the group member, explain the severe academic risk, and help them rewrite the content with proper citations before submission.
Report the incident directly to the instructor or evaluator to ensure your own integrity is not questioned.
Remove the plagiarised section yourself immediately without telling the member to protect the group deadline.
Leave it as it is since it was unintentional, but ensure future submissions are thoroughly reviewed.

scenario: You have an important exam tomorrow morning and a group project submission due tonight. A teammate who was supposed to compile the final slides falls ill and cannot finish.
question: How do you prioritize your remaining hours?
options: Communicate with the other healthy teammates to distribute the remaining slides equitably, finish them swiftly, and preserve study time for the exam.
Stay up late and complete the entire presentation by yourself, accepting lower preparation time for your exam.
Contact the teacher or professor immediately, explain the medical emergency, and request a brief extension for the project.
Submit the presentation in its current unfinished state with a note explaining the teammate's sudden illness.

scenario: A mentor or senior reviewer thoroughly critiques your recent project submission, pointing out several analytical flaws and recommending substantial structural changes.
question: How do you approach their critique?
options: Acknowledge their feedback with appreciation, ask clarifying questions to understand their perspective, and draft a structured revision plan.
Defend your original approach by presenting detailed arguments for why your initial decisions were valid.
Accept all changes passively without discussion and blindly implement whatever they recommended.
Feel demotivated and ask to be reassigned to a different project or mentor.

scenario: You are given a research assignment with very broad and ambiguous guidelines: 'Explore modern renewable energy transitions in developing nations' with no further rubric.
question: What is your best initial course of action?
options: Define a specific, manageable problem statement (e.g. solar microgrids in rural communities), outline your research methodology, and confirm it with the instructor.
Wait until the instructor provides more detailed criteria and specific questions before starting.
Look at what other students are doing and replicate their topics and structure closely.
Write a very general and high-level overview without focusing deeply on any specific aspect.

scenario: You have high aptitude and strong marks in Computer Science and Mathematics, but your family strongly encourages you to pursue Medicine, a field you feel less intrinsically drawn to.
question: How do you navigate this career decision?
options: Gather objective information on career pathways in CS/Tech, bioinformatics, and healthcare technology, and have an open, structured discussion with your family.
Immediately acquiesce to family expectations to avoid family conflict, setting aside your own interests.
Flatly refuse their recommendation and cut off communication regarding your career choices.
Postpone making any decision until the final day of college admission and let circumstances decide.

scenario: In a 4-person team project, one member consistently misses meetings and fails to contribute their assigned deliverables, putting the group grade at risk.
question: What is the most constructive response?
options: Have a private, direct conversation with the member to understand if they are facing personal hurdles, reiterate project expectations, and set mini-deadlines.
Immediately report them to the supervisor and request that their name be removed from the project.
Ignore the teammate, quietly absorb their workload among the remaining three, and harbor silent resentment.
Confront the member aggressively in front of the entire group during the next meeting to force accountability.

scenario: You prepared diligently for a prestigious scholarship exam or entrance competition for six months, but the final result falls just short of the cutoff score.
question: How do you recover from this setback?
options: Allow yourself a short time to process the disappointment, perform an honest analysis of weak areas, and identify alternative pathways with your existing preparation.
Decide that you lack academic talent and abandon all competitive career aspirations.
Blame the test format, evaluating authorities, and test conditions rather than reviewing your answers.
Immediately retake the exact same preparation routine without altering any strategies or study methods.

scenario: You are interning at a lab or company and realize you made an erroneous calculation in a client report that was already sent to senior management yesterday.
question: What step do you take?
options: Promptly notify your supervisor, present the corrected figures alongside a brief explanation of how the error occurred, and apologize professionally.
Wait and see if anyone notices; only address the error if a senior manager brings it up.
Quietly alter the master data file and pretend the original calculation was correct from the start.
Blame the calculation template provided by a colleague to deflect personal fault.

scenario: Halfway through a semester or project, the institution transitions from traditional software to a completely new digital collaboration platform that you have never used.
question: How do you approach the change?
options: Invest time over the weekend to explore documentation and video tutorials, test key features, and share helpful shortcuts with peers.
Complain to the administration that changing tools mid-project is disruptive and demand a rollback.
Use only the bare minimum features required and avoid learning the system's collaborative capabilities.
Ask a tech-savvy peer to complete your tasks on the new platform on your behalf.

scenario: A junior student or newcomer to your study club approaches you struggling with a fundamental concept you mastered months ago.
question: How do you respond to their request?
options: Spend 15–20 minutes walking them through an intuitive real-world example, then recommend a great resource for independent practice.
Send them your old notes without explanation and tell them to figure it out on their own.
Solve their homework problems directly for them so they finish quickly.
Politely tell them you are too busy and advise them to search the internet.

scenario: Your team's science exhibition project budget is suddenly cut in half, making the originally ordered mechanical parts unaffordable.
question: How do you adapt the project plan?
options: Hold a brainstorming session to redesign the prototype using recycled or low-cost materials without compromising core functionality.
Insist on continuing with the expensive design and ask team members to pay out of their personal pockets.
Abandon the project completely, arguing that high-quality science cannot be done with half a budget.
Reduce the project scope to a poster presentation without any working prototype.

scenario: You are selected to deliver the keynote presentation on behalf of your class at an inter-school conference, but public speaking makes you anxious.
question: How do you prepare for the event?
options: Prepare thoroughly, practice repeatedly in front of trusted friends and record yourself to build confidence and polish delivery.
Decline the invitation immediately and pass the opportunity to an extroverted classmate.
Show up on the day of the conference without rehearsal, hoping natural adrenaline will carry you through.
Read directly from a densely written manuscript without looking at the audience.

scenario: You are building a software prototype or design mock-up. You can either deliver an 80% polished product on time, or delay delivery by a week to make it 100% perfect.
question: What strategy do you choose?
options: Deliver the solid 80% version on schedule, clearly document known edge-cases, and outline a planned update roadmap.
Delay delivery by a week without consulting stakeholders, believing quality justifies missed deadlines.
Rush through the remaining 20% carelessly in the final two hours, introducing unvetted bugs.
Hand over only what you finished and refuse to work on the remaining features.

scenario: You notice an objective factual error in the project specifications provided by your senior professor or supervisor.
question: How do you address the discrepancy?
options: Request a brief one-on-one conversation, politely present the evidence or source data, and inquire about their thoughts on the discrepancy.
Point out the mistake publicly in front of the entire class or department to show your analytical sharpness.
Stay silent, follow the erroneous instruction, and let the project fail to prove the supervisor wrong.
Complain about the supervisor's competence to fellow students behind their back.
